content:
Elouan, Stoller Family Estate, and Chehalem may not be near one another (Elouan is in California and Chehalem is in Oregon), but all are part of the Stoller Wine Group, based in Oregon’s Willamette Valley.

Today we’re looking at three roses all made from Oregon pinot noir grapes, but representing two different vintages. Thoughts follow.

2024 Elouan Rose Oregon – “Grown in Oregon, made in California.” A pretty, strawberry-forward wine, this 100% pinot noir rose is laced with caramel and touched with floral notes, undercut with layers of lemon and mandarin orange. Juicy but refined, the wine finds a summery footing that meanders its way toward coconut and more tropical notes, concluding on a guava note. A total crowd-pleaser and a great value. A- / $15

2025 Chehalem Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – A considerably drier wine than the Elouan, this 2025 expression hits as rather more traditional, almost rustic at times, with stronger orchard notes of peach and apricot, fading gently into lemon and baked apple as the wine warms up a bit. Again, some coconut gives the finish some exoticism, but it’s much more restrained than the above wine. B+ / $21

2025 Stoller Family Estate Pinot Noir Rose Willamette Valley – Hard-edged at first blush, with a heavily herbal influence that tempers the natural fruit and florals in the mix. I never quite came around to this expression, which remains steadfastly greener than the other expressions in this roundup, and a little weedy at times. That said, a lime sherbet character on the finish perks things up a bit, particularly as the wine warms in glass. Doesn’t really evoke a rose. B / $15

title: Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026
summary:

Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release…

The post Review: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Since 2021, Japanese distillery Nikka has released regular special editions of single malts from its Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries, offering consumers a way to understand how the styles of the two distilleries compare and contrast.

Now, Nikka is at long last bringing back another, older Miyagikyo expression, one which went silent after its last release in 2014. For 2026, the whisky finally returns: Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old. The label has changed (and the price, of course, has gone up) but the song otherwise remains about the same, “crafted by Nikka Whisky’s current blending team, using carefully reserved whisky batches to ensure consistency and quality for future releases.” The subtext of that: More age statemented whiskies are on the way.

We were excited to get a sample from one of only 1572 bottles available in the U.S. Thoughts follow.

Nikka Miyagikyo 10 Years Old 2026 Review

Soft but pretty on the nose, the natural fruit of Miyagikyo comes through right away, It bursts with apple particularly but also finds room for notes of orange blossom and a bit of peach. Fragrant and summery, this isn’t as sweet-smelling as some previous Miyagikyo releases, offering more of a balanced aromatic profile that tempers its fruit with gentle notes of sandalwood and polished oak.

The palate offers similar and quite engaging flavors, apple, pear, and gentle coconut notes all well-represented. The apple notes feel fresh and inviting — red over green — layers of baking spice folded into the sip. The natural woodiness of the whisky is slowly revealed as it develops on the tongue, again sandalwood and silky layers of something darker linger underneath, owing to the influence of new American oak and some sherry staves. Elegant and always inviting throughout the experience, this feels like a much more mature whisky than it is finishing on a cleansing note while evoking a hint of vanilla and nougat.

90 proof.

A / $175 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: NV Sandeman Apitiv Reserve White Port appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In the U.S., white Port continues to grow in popularity — albeit haltingly — with options like Sandeman‘s Apitiv Reserve increasingly available. Made from white grape varietals including (in this case) Malvasia Fina, Códega, Viosinho, Rabigato, Arinto, and Gouveio, white Port is just as sweet as ruby or tawny varieties, but its flavor profile is completely different and much more summery.

Slightly darker in color than the typical white Port, this kicks off with ample sweetness that evokes peaches and pears, both fresh and tinned versions. A floral character adds a light astringency, featuring notes of rose petals and orange flowers. As the wine develops in glass, the fruit notes take on a more caramelized note, weaving into a flambeed banana character, pairing well with lingering tropical overtones. More intense than your typical white Port — just as the color would suggest — it’s a fine option for a refreshing white Port and tonic, or as an aperitif on its own.

A- / $25

title: Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum

But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail…

The post Review: Probitas Green Label Blended Rum appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Richard Seale has had an outsized role in the rum resurgence of the last twenty years. His Foursquare distillery helped move the category into the super-premium space after a long exile in beach bars and frat houses. But well-aged sippers like Foursquare’s Exceptional Cask Selections weren’t the only rums behind this renaissance. The corresponding cocktail boom, and rebirth of Tiki culture more specifically, gave equal weight to well-made mixing rums.

Launched in 2018, Probitas was designed to meet the cocktailing moment. The blend of Foursquare’s pot- and column-distilled rums from Barbados with pot-distilled rums from Hampden Estate in Jamaica became a go-to white rum cocktail base, adding depth to lighter Caribbean classics. Now the Probitas line is growing with a new addition that looks to fill the darker rum needs of backbars everywhere.

Like the original, Probitas Green Label is a blend of pot- and column-distilled rums. Specifically, it merges unaged twin-column coffey still rum, unaged double-retort pot still rum, and two-year aged double-retort pot still rum from Foursquare Rum Distillery in Barbados with unaged double-retort pot still rum from Hampden Estate. The big distinction appears to be the 10% increase in alcohol content and, perhaps even more significant, the addition of caramel coloring. But this isn’t the sugary, artificial stuff you would find in lower quality rums. How could it be? Richard Seale has been at the vanguard of the additive-free rum movement. As such, he created his own caramel coloring in house by superheating sugar, leaving zero residual sweetness to influence the natural flavors of the blend. Let’s check it out.

Probitas Green Label Blended Rum Review

While classic Probitas is bright and fruity on the nose, this Green Label expression is almost brooding with dark, rich notes of blackstrap molasses, overcooked caramel, and bruleed sugar. As it opens, a little baked pineapple manages to show itself before retreating into more caramelized sugars and an ester-heavy funk that seems even more pronounced than in the classic, despite all those darker sugary notes. With even more time in the glass, things coalesce into dark butterscotch and banana pudding.

The palate is potent, unsurprisingly given the significant uptick in proof, but a smack of brown sugar and cola instantly cools the ethanol and complements undertones of table syrup, clove-studded orange, and candied pineapple. It’s mouthcoating and wonderfully rich, tiptoeing dangerously close to syrupy but never quite getting there. The midpalate is peppery with a pronounced chicory coffee note that adds tannins and grip before eroding into silkier notes of Demerara syrup, five spice, and candied orange peel on a generous, warming finish. Where classic Probitas is ideal for a daiquiri, this new Green Label is a go-to for bolder Tiki drinks or a rum Old Fashioned.

114 proof.

A- / $35

The post Review: Four Peaks Kilt Lifter appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Four Peaks Brewing, based in Tempe, Arizona, got its start 30 years ago, making it an OG craft brewery. Kilt Lifter was the beer that put Four Peaks on the map, and it remains dominant today: Over the past three decades, Four Peaks has sold more than 800,000 barrels of it, or 200 million pints.

Nevertheless we’ve never covered it. In fact, I’ve never even tasted it until now. So, congrats on 30 years! Here’s a short review.

Ruddy and nutty, Kilt Lifter evokes the tartan on its can design with a bold attack of malt and well-toasted bread, landing somewhere between a savory slice of buttered toast and a breakfast pastry. A gently smokiness leans things toward the former, though the rounded body, a bit gummy at times, always threatens to push the experience back the other way. A finish that touches on vanilla caramel and baked apples makes for a nice counterpoint to some of the warmer elements in the mix. Definitely a winning pick for a cool afternoon.

6% abv.

A- / $12 per six-pack

The post Review: Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When it shipped in July 2026, the delay of the spring 2026 edition of Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond was hardly a surprise. These releases invariably hit the market at least a season too late, and Heaven Hill doesn’t seem overly concerned about changing the names of the whiskeys to align with reality.

The first release of 2026 is one of the younger wheated bourbon offerings in the series, all made from stock produced in the spring of 2016. Here we go.

Old Fitzgerald Bottled-in-Bond 10 Years Old Spring 2026 Edition Review

Old Fitzgerald has a reputation for softness, but this expression immediately strikes the nose as even quieter than typical, with the trademark brown banana dominant, layered lightly with cinnamon and nutmeg. A breakfast bowl of oatmeal is not far from the mark, complete with a lightly doughy character that furthers the impression of a morning meal.

The palate is extremely bright and pretty, a chewy dive into nougat and coconut cream, with layers of banana pudding dolloped on top. There’s a ton of vanilla present, all classic elements of the Old Fitz playbook (especially more youthful expressions like this). Hints of orange cream soda add some root beer notes add a more mid-afternoon quality to the experience, but it isn’t until late in the game when some more savory elements finally perk up, with just the lightest hints of barrel char, anise, and torched brassicas. The inherent sweetness of the whiskey fades into a slightly fruity quality on the finish, but only just so, leaving the consumer with an impression of Old Fitz at its absolute gentlest — at least so far.

100 proof.

A- / $150 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

As it’s been in the past the wine has an incredible density that suggests drinking it today is less than optimal. Nevertheless, a…

The post Review: 2023 Daou Soul of a Lion Cabernet Sauvignon Adelaida District appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This is our third round with Daou’s Soul of a Lion, the highest-end offering the Paso Robles winery produces. 2023’s release is 76% cabernet sauvignon, 18% cabernet franc, and 6% petit verdot.

As it’s been in the past the wine has an incredible density that suggests drinking it today is less than optimal. Nevertheless, a healthy decanting and some airtime can help this lion to temper its roaring a bit, pushing the 15.2% abv bruiser into gentler territory. After a bit of rest, the wine showcases flavors typical of the expression — raspberry and chocolate in a boozy, Port-like swirl, blackcurrants building as the finish digs its fingernails into you. The finish likens itself to a chocolate-coconut custard, doused in thick raspberry syrup. There’s no anise character to speak of with this expression, so if you’re looking for a more herbal wine this 2023 won’t do the trick. Those in need of a delightful pairing for that ribeye, however, need look no further.

A- / $160 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

summary:

Sure, it sounds more like a Twilight character than a 25 year old Canadian whisky — and even features an owl on the label — but whimsy like that has never stopped…

The post Review: Diageo Orphan Barrel Project Night Sage Canadian Whisky 25 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
I’ll hand it to Diageo and its Orphan Barrel Project: “Night Sage” is one of the most non-traditional and creative product names to date. Sure, it sounds more like a Twilight character than a 25 year old Canadian whisky — and even features an owl on the label — but whimsy like that has never stopped us from taking a product seriously.

Inside the bottle is a blended Canadian whisky with no clear provenance noted aside from being drawn from “the vast Diageo whisky inventory.” Distilled in Ontario and Manitoba, the whisky was matured in two different barrel types: “first-fill oak barrels, used only once prior, and multi-use barrels, both of which previously held other Canadian whisky.”

Let’s taste.

Diageo Orphan Barrel Project Night Sage Canadian Whisky 25 Years Old Review

Racier on the nose than its 45% abv would suggest, this pops with a surprising punch of pepper, both black and white, along with a perhaps telegraphed aroma of dried sage. An oxidized wine along the lines of oloroso sherry quickly makes an appearance, increasing in intensity as it develops in glass.

On the palate, again a boldly winey character quickly arrives, offering some of the doughy and buttery notes that are endemic to Canadian whisky. While a bit vegetal, a significant spice builds the longer you sit with it, resulting in a moderately floral, incense-laden midsection. The longer I sipped on this, the more it evoked perfume.

The finish finds the whisky leaning more into a vermouth character, the florals becoming quite dried and especially perfumy, even a little soapy at times. While it’s a bit much for my taste, that’s all par for the course for what is typically grain-heavy Canadian whisky, of course — and a sign that you are in fact getting what you paid for.

90 proof.

B+ / $225 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: 2024 Azevedo Loureiro Alvarinho Vinho Verde DOC appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Shop wisely and you can find this vinho verde for $10 or less, though it’s admittedly not the most expressive example of the style. Modest notes of lime inform a palate that leans on mango and guava rather than the brightly acidic citrus which vinho verde is known for. A little warmth helps the rather creamy wine to settle into a groove that finds a touch of minerality, enough to offset its occasionally gummy texture. Those tropical notes build to a crescendo on the finish, however, a burst of pineapple leading the way out.

B+ / $10

The post Review: Luxardo Espresso and Decaffeinated Espresso Liqueurs appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The trouble with the espresso martini (for me, anyway), isn’t the alcohol. It’s the caffeine. One of these in the evening and I’m up all night because I’m at that age.

Leave it to Luxardo to suggest the obvious: How about decaffeinating your coffee-flavored liqueur? That won’t do anything for the actual espresso you put in the drink — you’ll need a decaf version of that, too — but this will at least get you partway.

We’ve never reviewed the original Luxardo Espresso liqueur, so we’re doing double duty with this post and covering it and the decaf version (developed especially for the U.S. market) together.

Both are 54 proof.

Luxardo Espresso Liqueur Review

The nose is all dark-roast coffee beans and a touch of dark chocolate, quite intense without coming across as burnt. The palate offered quite a surprise as it struck me as very fruity, a mix of wine-soaked apples, cherry, and orange, reminding me a bit of a Cafe Brulot. The coffee character certainly isn’t shy, though the fruit and a significant amount of sugar evoke a confectionary quality as it sits on the tongue. The finish is quite sweet though at least shy of being overwhelming, with a last-gasp touch of vanilla-soaked chocolate syrup lingering. A- / $25 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Luxardo Decaffeinated Espresso Liqueur Review

The decaf version of the above has a slightly different presentation, but it’s not a dramatic departure from the original. The nose is not as strong as the caffeinated version, with a weaker coffee character, if only slightly. The intense, near-burnt notes of the original are absent; this noses more like a healthy brew of drip dark roast. The palate diverges a bit more, namely because the fruitier qualities of the original liqueur are nearly absent this go-round. In their stead, a stronger chocolate flavor and a more evident nuttiness, evoking hazelnut and pistachio. It seems even sweeter than the standard bottling, though knowing that there’s no caffeine in the product somehow makes it feel like a healthier choice. If you prefer a more chocolate-forward liqueur vs. a fruit-forward one, it’s the way to go between these two. A- / $30
